modules.title: Work with an AI coding agent
modules.description: Know what to delegate, what to read, and where your foundations help.

modules.title: Write prompts that move the work forward
modules.description: Turn an idea into a clear brief with focused context and observable outcomes.

modules.title: Give the interface a clear direction
modules.description: Connect user needs, visual references, hierarchy, and real interface states.

modules.title: Build one useful slice at a time
modules.description: Plan changes, reuse the project, debug with evidence, and keep useful checkpoints.

modules.title: Check what the agent actually built
modules.description: Review the diff, test behavior, and protect the people who will use the app.

modules.title: Finish a small app you can explain
modules.description: Keep context across sessions, make a release decision, and document your capstone.

lessons.title: You steer, the agent helps build
lessons.summary: Use the agent to turn decisions into code while you keep track of the result.
explanation: Vibe coding often starts with describing an idea in everyday language and letting an agent implement it. The useful habit is to keep a short loop: describe, inspect, try, and refine. You still decide whether the result solves the right problem.

An agent may generate a plausible explanation even when a button does nothing. Ask it to distinguish implemented work, checked behavior, and unfinished work. Read the output and try the feature yourself before accepting it.
lessons.example: Help me build a small study planner. First describe the user flow and propose one screen. After each implementation step, report what changed, what you checked, and what remains uncertain.
lessons.practice: Rewrite this prompt for an app you would actually use. Add one action you can verify in the running app.
lessons.question: The agent says the planner is complete, but you have not opened it. What should you do next?
options: Open the app and try the main user flow
Accept the completion message as proof
Ask for a longer completion message
lessons.answer: Open the app and try the main user flow
lessons.reason: A completion message is a claim. Trying the actual flow gives you evidence of what works.
lessons.hint: Choose the step that checks the product itself.

lessons.title: Know what your agent can access
lessons.summary: Match your request to the tools and permissions available in the session.
explanation: Some agents only suggest text. Others can read files, edit code, run commands, or inspect a browser. Those capabilities depend on the tool, session, and permissions. Ask what is available before requesting a task that depends on it.

Reading a repository and publishing it are different actions. Give a clear boundary for the current task, especially around deletion, production data, credentials, and deployment. A local preview is a useful first target for a new project.
lessons.example: Work in this project folder. Read the existing instructions and relevant files first. You may edit local source and run project checks. Ask before deleting data, changing account settings, or publishing anything. Report any tool you cannot access.
lessons.practice: List the actions your next task needs. Mark which require extra permission in your actual agent session.
lessons.question: A text-only assistant offers to verify your local browser without browser access. What is a reasonable response?
options: Treat its description as an observed browser result
Ask it to state the limitation and give checks you can run
Assume every agent has the same tools
lessons.answer: Ask it to state the limitation and give checks you can run
lessons.reason: Verification should match actual tool access. A checklist can help you check the browser when the agent cannot.
lessons.hint: Think about the evidence the tool can actually obtain.

lessons.title: Choose a first app you can finish
lessons.summary: Start with one useful flow and sample data you can understand.
explanation: A study planner with add, complete, and filter actions is a good first project. You can describe its data, try every action, and recognize a broken result. A marketplace with payments, roles, and live customer data adds many boundaries at once.
Write down what belongs in the first version and what can wait. Use local sample data before integrating services. A feature that is postponed should have no misleading button pretending to work.
lessons.example: Build version one of a study planner: add a task, mark it complete, and filter unfinished tasks. Use local sample data. Leave accounts, sync, payments, and notifications for later. Every visible action in this version must work.
lessons.practice: Pick three actions for your first app. Put every other idea into a later list.
lessons.question: Which first version gives you the clearest way to verify the result?
options: A marketplace with real payments and staff permissions
A social network with every feature on day one
A local task list with add, complete, and filter actions
lessons.answer: A local task list with add, complete, and filter actions
lessons.reason: A small local task list has a bounded flow and observable outcomes, making feedback and debugging easier.
lessons.hint: Choose a scope you can describe and try completely.

lessons.title: Use your coding foundations
lessons.summary: Knowing a little HTML, CSS, and JavaScript makes your feedback much more precise.
explanation: HTML explains structure, CSS explains layout, and JavaScript explains changing data and interactions. You can use an agent while learning these ideas. Understanding them helps you notice a clickable div, an overflowing layout, or state that never updates.

For this path, reading the brief lessons is open to everyone. Building and reviewing the capstone is easier after the HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and browser paths. Choose React or Next.js only when you can explain why the project needs them and follow the corresponding foundations.
lessons.example: Explain how this form uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Point to the relevant files and describe one input-to-view interaction. Keep the explanation beginner-friendly and give me one small change to try.
lessons.practice: Open a page you have built. Identify its structure, layout rules, and one event handler.
lessons.question: The task count stays at zero after adding an item. Which foundation is most directly useful?
options: JavaScript state and event handling
Choosing a new brand color
Adding more font families
lessons.answer: JavaScript state and event handling
lessons.reason: The count depends on the data update and rendering flow. JavaScript and browser foundations help you trace it.
lessons.hint: Look for the concept that connects an action with updated data.

lessons.title: Turn your idea into a product brief
lessons.summary: Tell the agent who needs the app, when they use it, and what they want to achieve.
explanation: “Build a planner” leaves the agent to guess the audience and workflow. “Help a student choose the next unfinished task during a short study break” gives the interface a job. The job tells you what should be visible and which action matters most.

Keep the brief short: audience, moment, main outcome, and the first useful flow. State important assumptions as assumptions. The agent can ask about an unresolved decision before turning a guess into a feature.
lessons.example: Product: a study planner for students with a 20-minute break. Goal: pick one unfinished task quickly. Main flow: see remaining tasks → add one if needed → mark it complete. First screen: task list and one add form. Ask about decisions that would change this flow.
lessons.practice: Write a four-line brief for your own app. Explain the user moment without listing UI decorations.
lessons.question: Which addition gives “build a planner” useful product context?
options: Make it impressive
Students use it during short breaks to pick one unfinished task
Use every modern UI trend
lessons.answer: Students use it during short breaks to pick one unfinished task
lessons.reason: Audience, moment, and outcome guide the layout and main action better than a vague style adjective.
lessons.hint: Look for a specific person doing a specific job.

lessons.title: Give your prompt a useful structure
lessons.summary: Combine a clear task, relevant context, constraints, and a way to check success.
explanation: A practical prompt answers four questions: what should change, what the agent needs to know, which boundaries apply, and how you will judge the result. You can use a few labeled lines. A role description such as “expert developer” alone does not supply these decisions.

Give the agent an output that supports the current step. For an unclear idea, ask for questions or a plan. For a scoped implementation, ask for the change and relevant verification. Avoid requesting pages of explanation when a short decision and a working feature are enough.
lessons.example:
Task: add a remaining-task filter.
Context: reuse the current task list and stable task IDs.
Constraints: preserve add/complete actions; no new dependency.
Success: filtering hides completed tasks; clearing the filter restores them.
Output: implement the change and report the checks you ran.
lessons.practice: Rewrite “make my app better” with these four parts and one observable success condition.
lessons.question: Your prompt says “act as an expert and make it great.” What is missing most?
options: More praise for the agent
A longer role description
A concrete task and observable success criteria
lessons.answer: A concrete task and observable success criteria
lessons.reason: A task and a checkable result give the agent a direction and give you a basis for review.
lessons.hint: Ask what you would actually try in the finished app.

lessons.title: Keep context relevant
lessons.summary: Provide the smallest set of reliable information that lets the agent do the task.
explanation: A longer prompt can still miss the important file, error, or user flow. Start with the current goal, relevant paths, existing conventions, and evidence. In a repository-aware agent, ask it to inspect the relevant files rather than pasting the entire codebase.

Remove repeated instructions and unrelated history. Preserve decisions that affect this task, especially constraints and verification. Context and token limits vary by tool, so treat concise relevance as a working habit rather than a guaranteed percentage of savings.
lessons.example: Fix only the task filter. Relevant files: task-list.js and task-list.test.js. Reproduce: complete a task, enable Remaining, then clear the filter; the task does not return. Expected: clearing restores the full list. Inspect these files and any directly related state code first.
lessons.practice: Take a long request you have written. Remove unrelated history while keeping the goal, evidence, and constraints.
lessons.question: Which context helps the agent investigate a broken filter most directly?
options: The relevant file paths and reproduction steps
The entire history of unrelated design changes
Many repeated requests to work harder
lessons.answer: The relevant file paths and reproduction steps
lessons.reason: Relevant paths and reproduction steps focus the investigation without filling the context with unrelated details.
lessons.hint: Choose information that narrows the problem.

lessons.title: Describe what working means
lessons.summary: Write acceptance criteria you can observe instead of asking for perfection.
explanation: “The form works” is broad. “Enter adds one trimmed title, whitespace-only input shows feedback, and focus remains usable” is testable. Include the happy path and an important failure or edge case.

Separate behavior from implementation preferences. “Use a button” may support keyboard access, but it is not proof that submitting works. Verify the interaction and result. If storage is part of the brief, define what survives reload and what happens when storage is unavailable.
lessons.example: Acceptance: Enter and the Add button each add exactly one task. Trim the title; reject an empty result with helpful feedback. Clear the input after success. Try empty input, spaces, and a normal title. Report the observed result for each.
lessons.practice: Write three checks for your main action, including one invalid input.
lessons.question: Which criterion is easiest to verify objectively?
options: The app should feel perfect
Submitting a whitespace-only title shows feedback and adds no task
The code should impress everyone
lessons.answer: Submitting a whitespace-only title shows feedback and adds no task
lessons.reason: The input, action, and expected outcome are explicit, so you can reproduce and verify the behavior.
lessons.hint: Look for a concrete action and result.

lessons.title: Start the design with a user flow
lessons.summary: Decide what users need to understand before choosing the visual treatment.
explanation: A first screen should explain where the user is, what they can do, and which step matters now. For a planner, the remaining tasks and the add action deserve more attention than decorative statistics. Sketch the entry, action, feedback, and next step in words.

Ask the agent to walk through the screen as a new user. A clear hierarchy may use spacing, alignment, headings, and one primary action. Choose a card or table because the content needs it; adding the same box around every section can flatten the hierarchy.
lessons.example: Review the first screen as a new student. Can they identify the remaining tasks and add a new one without guessing? Propose the content order and one primary action before changing styles. Keep the task list visible on a narrow screen.
lessons.practice: Describe a four-step user flow for your app. Identify what users should see at each step.
lessons.question: A planner opens with six decorative statistics and hides its tasks below the fold. What should guide the redesign?
options: Add more animation to the statistics
Put every section in an identical card
Prioritize choosing and adding tasks in the first screen
lessons.answer: Prioritize choosing and adding tasks in the first screen
lessons.reason: The layout should help the main user job. Showing the relevant tasks and action reduces unnecessary searching.
lessons.hint: Return to the user outcome in the brief.

lessons.title: Replace vague taste with visual decisions
lessons.summary: Explain layout, typography, spacing, and color in terms the agent can apply.
explanation: “Premium and modern” can produce a familiar template because it leaves every visual decision open. Give a direction: a compact task workspace, calm neutral surfaces, readable text, green for the main action, and dividers between groups. Explain why those choices help this user.

Use a small set of project tokens for type scale, spacing, color, and radius. Ask the agent to inspect existing tokens before adding values. The goal is a coherent interface with a deliberate identity; a particular color or rounded corner is not inherently bad.
lessons.example: Direction: a focused study workspace. Use the existing type scale and spacing tokens. Keep neutral surfaces; reserve the accent for the main action and meaningful state. Separate task groups with spacing and dividers. Explain any new visual treatment in terms of the user flow.
lessons.practice: Replace three vague adjectives in your design request with concrete decisions and their purpose.
lessons.question: Which instruction gives the agent an actionable visual direction?
options: Use existing spacing tokens and a readable task list with one accented main action
Make it super premium
Make it look like everything currently popular
lessons.answer: Use existing spacing tokens and a readable task list with one accented main action
lessons.reason: Concrete decisions constrain the design while tying the treatment to a task users need to complete.
lessons.hint: Choose instructions that describe an actual layout and hierarchy.

lessons.title: Use references with a reason
lessons.summary: Borrow useful design principles and create your own content and identity.
explanation: A screenshot can communicate density, composition, and hierarchy. Name the specific traits you want: the readable list rhythm, compact navigation, or strong heading alignment. Explain which parts do not fit your project so the agent does not copy the entire screen.

Use references you are allowed to share. Do not lift another product’s logo, proprietary assets, or fabricated testimonials. Your own real content and intended user flow should determine the resulting page. A reference is input for a decision, not proof that a design works for everyone.
lessons.example: Use this reference for its compact navigation and spacing between list rows. Create our own layout for study tasks using our existing tokens and real copy. Do not reuse its logo, imagery, or testimonials. Explain how the adapted hierarchy supports selecting the next task.
lessons.practice: Choose one reference and write down two useful traits and two parts you will not carry over.
lessons.question: Which reference request gives the clearest direction for an original result?
options: Copy the whole screen including its brand and claims
Adapt its compact list spacing to our tasks and existing tokens
Combine every section from five unrelated screenshots
lessons.answer: Adapt its compact list spacing to our tasks and existing tokens
lessons.reason: A named trait and a product-specific purpose guide adaptation while keeping the content and identity appropriate.
lessons.hint: Look for a specific trait connected to your own product.

lessons.title: Give every UI element a job
lessons.summary: Review generic output by asking how each part helps the user.
explanation: AI slop is often a mismatch between decoration and purpose: repeated cards, made-up statistics, loud gradients, or a hero that says little about the product. These patterns can be valid when they serve a real need. Review their contribution rather than banning a visual style.

Ask what each element helps the user find, understand, compare, or do. Remove unsupported proof and placeholders that pretend to work. Replace vague marketing language with real actions and content. Compare the result with your brief at both narrow and wide widths.
lessons.example: Audit this UI against our student task flow. For each decorative section, explain its user purpose or propose removing it. Replace invented metrics with real task data. Keep a clear main action, readable hierarchy, and the current product identity. Review narrow and wide layouts.
lessons.practice: Review one generated screen. Name one useful treatment and one element whose purpose you cannot explain.
lessons.question: A local planner displays “trusted by 10,000 students” with no supporting evidence. What should you request?
options: Make the claim bigger
Add a second invented testimonial
Remove the unsupported claim and use truthful product content
lessons.answer: Remove the unsupported claim and use truthful product content
lessons.reason: Unsupported proof misleads users. Useful real content is a better foundation for trust and design review.
lessons.hint: Think about whether the statement can be supported.

lessons.title: Ask for a plan when decisions matter
lessons.summary: Use a short plan to expose assumptions before a broad implementation.
explanation: A plan is helpful when the task touches several screens, data flows, or architectural decisions. Ask for the affected areas, proposed sequence, assumptions, and checks. For a small clear typo, a planning ceremony adds little value.

Review the plan for scope and dependencies. A first slice should run and support a real action. Resolve decisions that change the outcome, then let the agent implement that slice. A plan alone is not a working feature.
lessons.example: Before changing the planner, propose a short plan: affected files, data flow, assumptions, and verification. First slice: add and render one task. Identify any decision that blocks this slice. Once the plan is clear, implement the first slice and check it.
lessons.practice: Break a feature into three slices. Make sure each has a visible result you can try.
lessons.question: Which first slice provides useful implementation feedback?
options: Add and render one task, then check submission
Describe every possible future feature without building anything
Build every integration before the first screen runs
lessons.answer: Add and render one task, then check submission
lessons.reason: A runnable user action exposes real behavior early and gives the next iteration a stable starting point.
lessons.hint: Choose a small end-to-end action.

lessons.title: Let the project guide the implementation
lessons.summary: Ask the agent to inspect existing components, dependencies, and instructions before adding new ones.
explanation: An existing app already has decisions about routing, state, styles, and folder structure. Point the agent to project instructions and a relevant working feature. Reusing those contracts reduces accidental inconsistency.

A new dependency is justified by a concrete need, its tradeoffs, and how it fits the current stack. Ask for that reasoning before installing it. Do not replace the framework just to add a simple task filter.
lessons.example: Inspect project instructions, package.json, the current task component, and shared form styles. Add the filter using existing patterns. Explain if the current tools cannot meet a requirement before proposing a dependency or architecture change.
lessons.practice: Choose one existing component your next feature should reuse and explain the contract it provides.
lessons.question: The app already has a shared Button component. What is a useful first step for adding a filter action?
options: Install another complete UI kit immediately
Inspect and reuse the existing Button contract
Replace the application framework
lessons.answer: Inspect and reuse the existing Button contract
lessons.reason: Reusing an existing contract supports consistent behavior and styling without unnecessary dependencies.
lessons.hint: Check what the project already provides.

lessons.title: Give feedback the agent can act on
lessons.summary: Describe the location, observed behavior, expected outcome, and evidence.
explanation: “It looks wrong” leaves many possible changes. “At 390px, the Add button overlaps the input and hides its label” narrows the problem. If you share a screenshot, mention the relevant region and user action; an image alone may not explain the behavior.

Keep one feedback pass centered on a related problem. State what already works and the acceptance criteria for the fix. Compare the new result with the same scenario rather than judging a different screen or viewport.
lessons.example: On the task form at 390px wide, the Add button overlaps the input label. Keep submission behavior and the desktop layout. Stack the controls when space requires it. Check 390px and 1280px widths, long titles, and keyboard submission.
lessons.practice: Write feedback for one issue using location, actual result, expected result, and a repeatable check.
lessons.question: Which feedback gives the agent the most useful reproduction context?
options: Try harder to make it beautiful
Everything seems off
At 390px the Add button covers the label; keep the label visible and test submission
lessons.answer: At 390px the Add button covers the label; keep the label visible and test submission
lessons.reason: The viewport, location, problem, and expected result make the feedback actionable and checkable.
lessons.hint: Look for details you could repeat in the browser.

lessons.title: Debug with evidence
lessons.summary: Share the exact error and reproduction steps, then ask for the smallest justified fix.
explanation: An error prompt should include the command or action, exact message, relevant environment, and recent related changes. Remove secrets from logs before sharing. Ask the agent to form a hypothesis and inspect evidence before changing code.

A fix should address the cause and preserve the intended contract. Removing validation or deleting a test can hide a bug. Repeat the failing command and check the relevant user flow after the change. Report a blocker honestly if the environment prevents verification.
lessons.example: Reproduce: add a task, reload, then click Complete. Error: cannot read properties of undefined. Inspect the stored data shape and completion handler. Explain the cause, apply a focused fix, then test a new task, a reloaded task, and missing stored data. Do not remove validation to silence the error.
lessons.practice: Turn an error you have seen into a debugging prompt. Redact any private values first.
lessons.question: The agent proposes deleting the validation that exposes a malformed task. What should you ask for?
options: Inspect and fix the data mismatch, then repeat the failing flow
Delete every check until the console is quiet
Hide the error with CSS
lessons.answer: Inspect and fix the data mismatch, then repeat the failing flow
lessons.reason: Fixing the data contract addresses the cause. Silencing evidence can leave the broken behavior in place.
lessons.hint: Choose the action that repairs the cause.

lessons.title: Read the change before accepting it
lessons.summary: Use the diff to connect the requested behavior with the files the agent changed.
explanation: A diff shows added, removed, and edited lines. Ask the agent to explain why each affected area belongs to the task. Watch for unrelated rewrites, new dependencies, altered contracts, or checks that were weakened to pass.

If you cannot explain a change, ask about its input, output, and effect on the user flow. Review the current worktree before recording a version. Keep unrelated work intact and avoid broad reset commands while investigating.
lessons.example: Review the diff for the task filter. Explain the purpose of each changed file, any dependency or contract changes, and how add/complete still work. Identify unrelated edits before I accept the change. Summarize the relevant checks and their actual results.
lessons.practice: Read a small diff in your project. Explain one changed line in terms of its effect on the user.
lessons.question: A filter task also rewrites authentication and removes failing tests. What deserves review first?
options: Whether the completion message is enthusiastic
Why those unrelated changes were made and whether they are justified
The total number of added lines only
lessons.answer: Why those unrelated changes were made and whether they are justified
lessons.reason: Unrelated changes and weakened checks can create regressions. Review their purpose and impact before accepting them.
lessons.hint: Think about scope and contracts.

lessons.title: Test the flow beyond a build
lessons.summary: Check real actions, empty states, invalid inputs, and persistence when it is promised.
explanation: A successful build checks whether the project can compile and bundle. It does not prove that Add works, a filter restores items, or a reload keeps data. Use the project’s existing tests and inspect the actual running user flow.

List the expected outcome before trying each case. Include an empty list, whitespace input, a long title, completion, filter clearing, and reload if persistence is in scope. The agent should report which checks ran and which need your manual follow-up.
lessons.example: Run the project checks and verify this flow in the running app: add a trimmed title, reject spaces, complete a task, filter remaining items, and clear the filter. Test empty and long-title states. If storage is implemented, reload and check the data. Record expected and observed outcomes.
lessons.practice: Make a five-case check table for your app with input, action, and expected result.
lessons.question: The build passes, but clearing the filter never restores completed tasks. What does this show?
options: The browser must be ignored because the build passed
Passing a build proves all user flows
The build passed while a user behavior still needs fixing
lessons.answer: The build passed while a user behavior still needs fixing
lessons.reason: Compilation and user behavior are different checks. The failing interaction still needs investigation.
lessons.hint: Consider what a build actually verifies.

lessons.title: Make keyboard use part of the brief
lessons.summary: Ask for semantic controls, visible labels, focus, and useful feedback.
explanation: A clickable element should use the appropriate native control. Forms need labels, focus must remain visible, and status feedback should be understandable without color alone. These requirements belong in the implementation brief rather than a late visual polish pass.

Try Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, and Space where appropriate. Check the focus order and whether users can leave every control. Automated tools can catch some defects, but a score is not proof of complete accessibility. Review semantics and actual interactions too.
lessons.example: Use a labeled form and native buttons. Preserve visible focus indicators. Make adding and completing tasks work from the keyboard. Announce useful status feedback without relying only on color. Check focus order and that every control can be entered and exited with Tab.
lessons.practice: Use only the keyboard to add and complete a task. Note any point where focus disappears or gets stuck.
lessons.question: A styled div responds only to mouse clicks for completing a task. What is the better request?
options: Use an appropriate native control and check keyboard activation
Hide the focus ring everywhere
Add an animation to the div
lessons.answer: Use an appropriate native control and check keyboard activation
lessons.reason: A native control provides semantics and expected keyboard behavior; the interaction still needs to be checked.
lessons.hint: Think about operation beyond the mouse.

lessons.title: Review small screens and real content
lessons.summary: Test layout with narrow space, long text, and the assets the app actually needs.
explanation: Responsive work means deciding what stacks, wraps, remains visible, and changes priority. A screenshot of an empty desktop page says little about a long task title on a phone. Try narrow and wide layouts with realistic content and keyboard focus.

Performance improvements need evidence. Ask the agent to inspect initial loading, heavy assets, or a slow interaction before proposing a library or rewrite. Reuse existing tools, remove unnecessary work, and compare the same scenario before and after a change.
lessons.example: Review the planner at 390px and 1280px with empty, short, and long titles. Keep the main action and labels usable without horizontal overflow. Inspect unnecessary assets and dependencies before optimizing. Report measurements or observations rather than claiming a speedup without evidence.
lessons.practice: Test your longest likely content at two widths. Record a layout problem and one evidence-based improvement.
lessons.question: The agent claims “twice as fast” after changing colors and reports no measurement. How should you treat the claim?
options: Accept it because a visual change always improves speed
Ask for a relevant before-and-after measurement or observation
Repeat the claim in the product headline
lessons.answer: Ask for a relevant before-and-after measurement or observation
lessons.reason: A performance claim needs evidence from a comparable scenario. A color change alone does not establish a speedup.
lessons.hint: Look for evidence of the claimed outcome.

lessons.title: Keep secrets and production actions explicit
lessons.summary: Use sample data and deliberate permission boundaries as your app grows.
explanation: Do not place API secrets in browser code or paste private keys into a prompt. Use redacted logs and fake data for learning. A variable name or environment prefix does not automatically make a value private; browser-delivered values can be inspected.

When a project introduces accounts, payments, or production data, review those boundaries separately. Hiding a button is not server authorization. Keep the first planner local and ask before publishing, deleting data, or changing sensitive settings.
lessons.example: Use synthetic task data. Do not add secrets to client code or logs. Keep this change local. Identify any production, account, or data-deletion action before executing it, and request specific permission for that action.
lessons.practice: Review your planned integrations. Identify one secret or sensitive action and where its boundary belongs.
lessons.question: The agent suggests placing a private API key in the client bundle. What should happen?
options: Hide the key with a longer variable name
Trust the key because the source file is not linked from the homepage
Keep the secret out of browser-delivered code and review a server boundary
lessons.answer: Keep the secret out of browser-delivered code and review a server boundary
lessons.reason: Client-delivered values are accessible to users. Private credentials require an appropriate server-side boundary.
lessons.hint: Think about what the browser receives.

lessons.title: Carry useful context into the next session
lessons.summary: Save decisions, verified work, and the next task in a compact handoff.
explanation: A new session may not know why the app uses local data or which behavior was checked. Keep a handoff with the goal, project instructions, decisions, affected files, actual checks, unresolved issues, and one next step.

Distinguish completed from verified work. A session summary can contain mistakes, so ask the next agent to inspect the current files and worktree. Do not fill the handoff with unrelated chat history or secrets.
lessons.example:
Handoff:
Goal: local study planner.
Decisions: one task list; no accounts or remote sync.
Done: add, complete, remaining filter.
Verified: submission and filter clearing in the local browser.
Open: long titles overflow at 390px.
Next: inspect current worktree and fix that layout without changing behavior.
lessons.practice: Write a handoff for your current project in fewer than ten lines. Separate made, checked, and remaining work.
lessons.question: Which handoff helps a new agent resume responsibly?
options: Goal, decisions, verified checks, unresolved issue, and next task
Only “everything is done”
Every unrelated message from earlier conversations
lessons.answer: Goal, decisions, verified checks, unresolved issue, and next task
lessons.reason: A compact factual handoff preserves the decisions and evidence that the next task depends on.
lessons.hint: Look for facts the next task needs.

lessons.title: Make a release decision with evidence
lessons.summary: Review a small release against its promised flow and document known limits.
explanation: Before publishing, repeat the main flow in the production build or preview and review the relevant project checks. Confirm labels, links, error feedback, narrow layouts, and data behavior. Write down known limitations such as browser-only storage or no account sync.

Publishing changes a remote environment. Decide who authorizes it and how you will verify the live result and recover from a bad release. An agent should prepare a reviewable build and report blockers before that action.
lessons.example: Prepare a release review for the planner. Check the production preview, main task flow, keyboard use, narrow layout, and storage limits. List actual results and unresolved issues. Prepare the deployment steps and a recovery approach; wait for my authorization before publishing.
lessons.practice: Write a short release note with one verified behavior, one known limit, and a recovery action.
lessons.question: The agent has prepared a local build but has no permission to deploy. What is the correct next action?
options: Publish because the build passed
Present the checked result and request authorization to publish
Delete the existing deployment first
lessons.answer: Present the checked result and request authorization to publish
lessons.reason: A ready local artifact supports a release decision, while publishing still requires authorization for the remote action.
lessons.hint: Separate preparation from the remote action.

lessons.title: Build your Study Sprint capstone
lessons.summary: Bring your brief, prompt, visual direction, implementation, and review together.
explanation: Study Sprint is a small app for picking the next study task. Build three slices: add and render tasks, complete and filter them, then improve feedback and narrow layouts. Use an AI coding agent in your own local project; this site helps you prepare prompts and record your review.

Start with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript if you are still learning frameworks. React or Next.js is an option after its foundations, with the same user-facing acceptance criteria. In the project workspace, record the brief, prompts, decisions, real checks, and limitations. Completing a quiz does not verify the external app.
lessons.example: Build Study Sprint for a student choosing one task during a short break. First propose a brief and three implementation slices. Use the current project stack and a focused visual direction. Include add, complete, remaining filter, empty feedback, and keyboard use. Verify each slice and report evidence. Keep deployment separate until authorized.
lessons.practice: Open the course project workspace after the knowledge check. Build the app locally and record your actual prompts and observed results.
lessons.question: Which artifact best demonstrates what you learned in this capstone?
options: A screenshot alone with no working interactions
A long prompt without any result review
A working small app with the brief, decisions, and observed checks
lessons.answer: A working small app with the brief, decisions, and observed checks
lessons.reason: The app and review connect the requested outcome to implementation decisions and evidence.
lessons.hint: Choose work that connects intention with a tried result.
